messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Fatima was seven years old the first time her father threw a shoe at her head. It missed, but the pattern did not: a stinging slap for speaking out of turn, a belt for forgetting a chore, hours locked in a dark closet for reasons she never fully understood. By the time she left home at eighteen, she had learned that the world was a place where people who were supposed to protect you could hurt you instead—and that the institutions and community that should have intervened had looked away. She carried that lesson into adulthood, and it became the lens through which she saw everything: the world is dangerous, and those in power, whether the shipping company or her own family, could not be trusted.

Now fifty-three and a ship captain—a job that demands constant vigilance over crew and cargo—Fatima cannot shake the feeling that danger is always near. She monitors the entrances to her own home, listening for footsteps that might mean someone is forcing their way in. At night, her vigilance sharpens. She finds it nearly impossible to relax even when she knows she is secure, checking locks twice and sleeping in shallow, broken stretches. She has come to believe that the external world is hostile and that no one will protect her, so she must protect herself, and the only way to do that is to never let her guard down. This belief drives her to scan her environment obsessively for signs of threat—a sound in the hallway, a door left ajar—and her mind, wired by the past, fills in the rest.

Her memory of the abuse is fragmented yet emotionally potent. Sometimes Fatima feels the full terror and shame of a beating without being able to picture a single detail—a wave of helplessness that rises from nowhere, unmoored from any image. At other moments, she can recall the events clearly but feels nothing, as though the child who was hurt is a stranger she knows only by report. Most often, however, the memories come as vivid pictures: the grain of the closet door, the angle of a hand mid-swing. These visual intrusions flood into her mind, and then the negative appraisals rush in with them—the certainty that the world is dangerous, that she has been abandoned by her culture and community, that systems designed to protect children failed her. That sense of betrayal makes the memories feel more real and more threatening, confirming what she already knows.

She tries to push the memories away. Fatima suppresses thoughts of the trauma deliberately, turning her mind to navigational charts or engine maintenance whenever a flashback approaches. She also dwells on how the event could have been prevented—if only she had been quieter, faster, smarter—and on how she used to be before the abuse, a child who laughed freely. These ruminations, meant to gain control, instead loop back into more memories. The more she tries not to think about the trauma, the more the fragmented images surface, and the more she is reminded of her lost childhood and the failure of the institutions around her. That, in turn, feeds her hypervigilance: if she had stayed alert enough as a child, maybe she could have dodged the abuse; now, she must keep watch constantly to avoid any future danger. Her inability to relax is both a result of this monitoring and a cause of it—her body stays locked in a state of readiness, which triggers more scanning, which yields more memories.

The cycle has reshaped her life. At work, she is respected and competent, but she avoids any port with a Middle Eastern community that might remind her of the culture she lost during the abuse; she now feels no connection to the traditions she once loved, and the avoidance has left her isolated from old friends. She finds herself skipping crew social events because the unpredictable noise makes her feel unsafe. Her marriage has suffered—she is irritable, always on edge, unable to settle into shared downtime. Her husband tries to comfort her, but she cannot believe him; the people who should have protected her let her down, so why would he be any different?

She finally sought help after a deckhand walked up behind her unexpectedly and she wheeled around, nearly striking him. The incident terrified her. She came to the clinic saying she is afraid she is losing control of her mind and her career. What she wants most is to sleep through the night without listening for footsteps—but what she fears most is that if she stops watching, the world will prove her right.
